messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 69
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Financial Analyst
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 74

He comes to therapy as a 69-year-old widower who has built a life around numbers, forecasts, and disciplined routines, yet he describes the past year as something he can no longer quantify or control. For most of his adult life, he has worked as a financial analyst, and even now he keeps a careful calendar, reads market reports before breakfast, and finds comfort in orderly spreadsheets. That structure, he says, used to make sense of the world. Since the traumatic loss of his wife, it feels more like a scaffold holding up a life that has been hollowed out.

His wife dies unexpectedly after a brief and frightening medical crisis. He describes the days around her decline in painstaking detail, as if he is still trying to reconstruct the sequence correctly. He remembers the hospital room lights, the smell of antiseptic, the clipped voices of staff, and the moment he realizes that the person he has shared his life with for more than four decades is slipping away. He says he was not prepared for how quickly everything would change. One day he is discussing dinner plans and retirement travel; the next he is signing forms, making calls, and trying to understand words he cannot absorb. He repeatedly returns to the scene in his mind, especially to the look on her face in those final hours, and he speaks of it with a pained steadiness that breaks only when his voice tightens and he looks away.

After her death, he tries to return to work almost immediately, believing that staying busy will keep him afloat. Instead, the office becomes one more place where his concentration fails him. He sits in meetings unable to track what people are saying. He rereads the same reports and finds that the numbers blur. He has spent his career evaluating risk, yet now he feels ambushed by ordinary moments: a colleague mentioning a spouse, a voicemail left too early in the morning, a chair pulled up beside his desk. He remains outwardly competent, but he says it takes nearly all of his energy to appear that way. At home, he moves through the apartment with a sense that something essential has been removed. He keeps expecting to hear her in the kitchen or see her shoes by the door, and each time he remembers that she is gone, the realization lands as if newly inflicted.

He avoids the hospital route whenever possible, and he has begun to decline invitations that involve family gatherings or other couples. He says the world feels unfairly full of reminders. Photographs are difficult; he can look at them only briefly before putting them away. Some days he leaves the house and finds himself standing in the grocery store without remembering why he came. Other days he stays inside, sitting in silence with the television on for company, though he rarely follows what is happening on the screen. Sleep has become fragmented. He falls asleep from exhaustion and then wakes before dawn with his mind immediately returning to the moment of loss. In those early hours, he often sits in the dark and reviews what he could have done differently, even though he knows, rationally, that the outcome was not something he controlled. The self-reproach is persistent anyway.

He speaks of guilt in a restrained way that suggests how familiar it has become. He wonders whether he should have noticed something sooner, pushed harder for another opinion, been more present in the hospital, spoken more carefully in the weeks before her illness. These thoughts do not come as occasional doubts; they arrive like an internal audit, as if he is balancing accounts that will never reconcile. He reports feeling emotionally numb much of the time, then suddenly overwhelmed when a memory breaks through. He can become tearful without warning, especially when he hears a song they liked or passes a place they used to visit together. At other times he feels detached from people around him, observing their lives with a distance that surprises him. Friends tell him to “keep busy” or “move on,” and he nods, but privately he feels that language does not fit what has happened. Moving on sounds, to him, like a betrayal.

Despite this, he continues to function in a careful, narrowed way. He goes to work, pays bills on time, and maintains the household as best he can. He is the kind of man who still checks the lock twice and reviews the day’s schedule before bed, not because he expects things to be fine but because he needs the smallest possible sense of control. He says he does not feel like the same person who once planned for retirement with optimism. Instead, he lives alongside grief that arrives in waves, reshaping ordinary moments into reminders of what has been taken from him.
